name: Absolute zero
funFact: Absolute zero is the coldest theoretically possible temperature — at this point all molecular motion stops. Physicists have cooled substances to within a billionth of a degree of absolute zero but can never actually reach it.

name: Aluminium melting
funFact: Aluminium melts at 660°C but was more expensive than gold in the 1800s because it was so difficult to extract. Napoleon III served honoured guests with aluminium cutlery; less important guests had to make do with gold and silver.

name: Antarctic winter
funFact: At −60°C exposed skin freezes in under a minute and exhaled breath freezes before it disperses. The record low at the South Pole station is −82.8°C — cold enough that steel becomes brittle and shatters like glass.

name: Battery thermal runaway
funFact: Thermal runaway is a self-amplifying process — the heat causes more chemical reactions, which release more heat. Once started it's essentially unstoppable, which is why exploding phone batteries can burn through metal.

name: Body temperature
funFact: The 37°C standard was set by German physician Carl Wunderlich in 1851 after measuring 25,000 patients — modern studies suggest the true average is closer to 36.6°C.

name: Boiling water
description: Water boiling point at sea level = 100°C.
funFact: 100°C is the anchor of the Celsius scale — Anders Celsius originally defined it as the freezing point, not boiling, and had 0 at boiling. A colleague reversed it after his death, which is why cold is 0 and hot is 100.

name: CPU thermal throttle
funFact: Intel and AMD CPUs automatically reduce clock speed at ~95°C and shut down entirely at ~105°C. The thermal management software in a modern CPU makes thousands of decisions per second about clock speed and voltage.

name: Candle flame
funFact: A candle flame has four distinct zones — the cool dark inner cone, a warm luminous zone, a hot outer cone, and an invisible outer veil of hot gases.

name: Car interior (summer)
description: Parked car interior on a hot day ≈ 60–70°C.
funFact: A car interior can reach 65°C on a 35°C day in just 20 minutes with windows closed. At this temperature, steering wheels can cause burns, chocolate melts, and aerosol cans can explode.

name: Cast iron sear
description: Optimal cast iron searing temperature ≈ 230 °C (503.15 K).
funFact: The perfect sear happens at 230°C because that's where the Maillard reaction — the chemical process that creates browning and flavour — runs fastest without burning. Below 150°C the reaction barely happens. Above 260°C you get charring instead. The sweet spot is surprisingly narrow for something every culture figured out independently.

name: Comfortable bath
funFact: 40°C is 3°C above body temperature — warm enough to relax muscles without raising your core temp dangerously. Any hotter and your heart rate increases to compensate.

name: Comfortable room
funFact: The 21°C comfort standard was largely set by office building HVAC systems designed in the 1960s for men in suits — many women consistently report feeling too cold at this temperature.

name: Deep space
funFact: The cosmic microwave background radiation is the afterglow of the Big Bang — and at 2.7 Kelvin, it's the coldest large-scale temperature in the known universe.

name: Dry ice
funFact: Dry ice skips the liquid phase entirely — solid CO₂ sublimates directly to gas. The dramatic fog effect in concerts and theatres is CO₂ gas chilling the surrounding air and condensing its moisture into visible droplets.

name: Freezer
funFact: The −18°C standard for home freezers was set in the 1930s by Clarence Birdseye, who discovered that flash-freezing food at this temperature preserved texture far better than slow freezing. He got the idea from watching Inuit fishermen in Labrador freeze fish almost instantly in −40°C Arctic air.
exampleMeme: Where leftovers go to be forgotten.

name: Fresh fast food fries
description: Fresh McDonald's fries out of the fryer ≈ 80°C.
funFact: McDonald's fries are cooked at 168°C and served at around 80°C. The company's internal standards require fries to be discarded if not served within 7 minutes — which is why fresh fries are always hotter than you expect.

name: Freshly baked bread
description: Internal temperature of freshly baked bread ≈ 95 °C (368.15 K).
funFact: Professional bakers determine doneness by internal temperature, not colour or time — bread is done at exactly 93-96°C internally, regardless of what the crust looks like. At this temperature, the starches have fully gelatinised and the proteins have set. Every degree matters: pull it at 88°C and the centre will be gummy.
exampleMeme: The smell is the best thermometer.

name: GPU thermal throttle
description: High-end GPU under full load before throttling ≈ 90°C.
funFact: Modern GPUs can execute over 100 trillion floating-point operations per second. At 90°C they automatically reduce performance to prevent damage — a process called thermal throttling that can cut performance by up to 30%.

name: High fever
funFact: Fever is the immune system deliberately raising body temperature to make conditions hostile for bacteria and viruses, most of which can't function well above 38°C.

name: Jet engine exhaust
funFact: Jet engine turbine blades operate inside a gas stream hotter than their own melting point — they survive only because of hollow internal cooling channels that pump cool air through the blade, essentially air-conditioning each blade individually.

name: Laptop on your lap
description: Underside of a laptop under load ≈ 50–60°C.
funFact: Laptop manufacturers officially advise against using laptops on soft surfaces like beds and laps. The name 'laptop' predates widespread heat issues — modern devices generate so much heat that Apple calls the MacBook a 'notebook computer' specifically to discourage lap use.

name: Lava
funFact: Despite being over 1,000°C, lava moves slowly enough that humans can outrun it on foot — most lava-related deaths come from toxic gases, not the lava itself.

name: Lightning bolt
description: Temperature of a lightning bolt channel ≈ 30,000°C.
funFact: A lightning bolt is approximately 5 times hotter than the surface of the Sun — yet it lasts only 30 microseconds. The rapid superheating of air causes the explosive expansion we hear as thunder, travelling outward at the speed of sound.
exampleMeme: Five times hotter than the Sun.

name: Liquid nitrogen
funFact: Liquid nitrogen is so cold that a small amount poured onto your skin rapidly boils away before it can cause a burn — a phenomenon called the Leidenfrost effect. However, holding it for more than a second causes severe frostbite.

name: Liquid oxygen
funFact: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and strongly magnetic. The Space Shuttle's main engines burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, consuming about 500,000 litres of propellant in the first two minutes of flight.

name: Nuclear reactor core
description: Nuclear reactor fuel rod operating temperature ≈ 2,500–3,000°C.
funFact: A nuclear reactor fuel rod sits at 2,750°C — hotter than the surface of the Sun. The entire system is engineered so that if control is lost, the physics of fission naturally cause the reaction to slow down, a property called a 'negative temperature coefficient.'

name: Paper ignition
funFact: Ray Bradbury named his novel Fahrenheit 451 (233°C) after the temperature at which paper ignites. The actual auto-ignition temperature of paper varies from 218–246°C depending on the paper type — Bradbury's figure is approximately correct.

name: Perfect coffee
funFact: The Specialty Coffee Association recommends serving espresso between 59–63°C. Studies show taste perception for bitterness and sweetness changes significantly with temperature — the same coffee tastes different at 40°C vs 60°C.

name: Phone overheating warning
funFact: Apple officially states iPhones should be used between 0°C and 35°C. At 45°C the battery charges more slowly, at 60°C it stops charging entirely to prevent damage.
exampleMeme: Temperature too high. Please cool device.

name: Pizza oven
funFact: A Neapolitan pizza cooks in exactly 60–90 seconds at 450°C — any longer and the crust burns, any shorter and it's raw.

name: Refrigerator
funFact: 4°C is the temperature at which water is densest — a coincidence that makes it the international standard for food-safe cold storage. It's also the temperature of the deep ocean.

name: Sauna
funFact: Finland has 3.3 million saunas for 5.5 million people — roughly one per household. The Finnish word 'sauna' is one of very few Finnish words adopted into English virtually unchanged.

name: Skin pain threshold
description: Temperature where heat becomes painful to touch ≈ 43°C.
funFact: At exactly 43°C, human TRPV1 heat receptors activate and signal pain. This same receptor detects capsaicin in chilli peppers — which is why spicy food literally feels hot.

name: Spacecraft re-entry
description: Heat shield temperature during atmospheric re-entry ≈ 1,650°C.
funFact: The Space Shuttle's heat shield tiles could be held by their edges while glowing orange-hot in the centre — they dissipated heat so quickly that only the surface was scorching. Astronauts were sitting just centimetres away from 1,650°C.

name: Steel softening
funFact: The collapse of the World Trade Center towers was not caused by the fires melting the steel, but by steel softening at 600°C — enough to make the floor trusses sag and trigger progressive collapse. Steel doesn't need to melt to fail structurally.

name: Sun's core
description: Temperature at the core of the Sun ≈ 15,000,000°C.
funFact: The Sun's core is 15 million°C — hot enough to fuse hydrogen nuclei into helium despite their electromagnetic repulsion. A single photon of light generated there takes 100,000 years to reach the surface, bouncing between particles the whole time.

name: Sun's surface
funFact: The Sun's corona (outer atmosphere) is paradoxically hotter than its surface — reaching over 1,000,000°C — a mystery that still isn't fully explained.

name: Surface of Venus
funFact: Venus is actually hotter than Mercury despite being further from the Sun. Its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat so effectively that the surface sits at 465°C — hot enough to melt lead — at all times, day or night.
exampleMeme: Hotter than the planet closer to the Sun.

name: Swimming pool
funFact: Olympic competition pools are kept at exactly 25–28°C. Warmer water makes swimmers tire faster; cooler water causes muscles to cramp.
exampleMeme: Warm enough to stay, cool enough to swim.

name: Welding arc
funFact: The electric arc in welding is hotter than the surface of the Sun. Welding helmets must block 99.99% of UV and IR radiation — the intense light would cause permanent retinal damage in under a second without protection.
